# Supraventricular tachycardia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Arrhythmias > Supraventricular tachycardia*

[Original Article Link](/library/FS0gYf)

---

## Summary

Supraventricular tachycardias (SVTs) are a group of <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> arising from abnormalities in pacemaker activity and/or conduction involving <u>myocytes</u> of the <u>atria</u> and/or <u>AV node</u>. Types of SVT include <u>atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia</u> (<u>AVNRT</u>; approx. two-thirds of cases), <u>atrioventricular reciprocating tachycardia</u> (<u>AVRT</u>), <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u> (FAT), <u>multifocal atrial tachycardia</u> (<u>MAT</u>), and <u>junctional tachycardia</u>. <u>AVNRT</u> and <u>AVRT</u> are caused by abnormal conduction circuits that form an unending loop of conduction referred to as reentry. These reentry circuits can occur between parallel pathways within the <u>AV node</u> (as in <u>AVNRT</u>) or between the <u>AV node</u> and an <u>accessory pathway</u> of atrioventricular conduction (as in <u>AVRT</u>). Atrial tachycardias (FAT and <u>MAT</u>) and <u>junctional tachycardias</u> are usually the result of abnormal or <u>ectopic pacemaker</u> activity and do not involve reentry. The most common congenital <u>accessory pathway</u> (<u>bundle of Kent</u>) is seen in <u>Wolff-Parkinson-White</u> (<u>WPW</u>) syndrome and can cause <u>ventricular preexcitation</u>, in which supraventricular impulses bypass the <u>AV node</u> and are abnormally conducted to the ventricles, leading to a characteristic <u>preexcitation pattern</u> on <u>ECG</u> and a specific subset of <u>preexcited tachyarrhythmias</u>. SVTs have similar clinical features (typically paroxysms of <u>tachycardia</u> with <u>dizziness</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>chest pain</u>, or <u>syncope</u>) that may be <u>self-limiting</u> or progress to <u>hemodynamic instability</u> and <u>sudden cardiac death</u>. Common diagnostic steps include obtaining the patient's history and a 12-lead <u>ECG</u> to identify the type of SVT. The <u>paroxysmal</u> nature of SVTs means that continuous recording with a <u>Holter monitor</u> is often needed to confirm the diagnosis; in some cases, invasive <u>electrophysiological studies</u> (<u>EP studies</u>) may also be indicated. <u>Management of SVT</u> should be tailored to the patient. Most <u>hemodynamically unstable</u> patients are treated with emergency <u>cardioversion</u>, while patients with acute SVT episodes that are hemodynamically stable may benefit from <u>vagal maneuvers</u> and/or <u>antiarrhythmic medication</u> (typically intravenous), depending on the underlying rhythm. Long-term management may involve <u>antiarrhythmic medication</u> or curative <u>catheter ablation</u>.




The following are discussed in detail separately: “<u>Management of tachycardia</u>,” “<u>Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response</u>” and “<u>Atrial flutter</u>.“

---

## Definitions

### Tachycardias




* Paroxysmal tachycardia: an <u>arrhythmia</u> with an abrupt onset and termination that can last from seconds to days (e.g., <u>AVNRT</u>)  [[1]](/library/4hb3Vt)

* Supraventricular <u>tachycardia</u> (SVT)

* A <u>tachycardia</u> originating in the following:  [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[3]](/library/khbmVt)

* Sinus node

* <u>AV node</u>

* Atrial <u>myocardium</u>

* <u>Bundle of His</u> above the bifurcation

* Includes:

* Reentrant tachycardias: e.g., <u>AVNRT</u>, <u>AVRT</u>

* Atrial tachycardias: <u>focal AT</u>, <u>multifocal AT</u>, <u>Afib</u>, <u>Atrial flutter</u>

* <u>Inappropriate sinus tachycardia</u>

* <u>Junctional tachycardia</u>

* Paroxysmal SVT (<u>PSVT</u>)

* Any SVT with a <u>narrow QRS complex</u> and an abrupt onset

* Most commonly caused by <u>AV nodal reentry</u>





### Conduction abnormalities




#### Reentry




* A mechanism that causes an impulse in the <u>heart</u> (which would normally die out) to return via conduction circuit to reexcite the tissue, leading to an extra beat (or, if it continues, an ongoing <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>) [[4]](/library/OhbIVt)[[5]](/library/lhbvVt)

* Examples of reentrant tachycardias include <u>AVNRT</u> and <u>AVRT</u>.





![Cardiac reentry mechanism](media/prohr72jbikqkzvz6p40bwho.jpg)

Cardiac reentry mechanism

![Pathophysiology of typical atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)](media/ryso4djvece1mlsv7pqa39nh.jpg)

Pathophysiology of typical atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)




#### Aberrant conduction [[6]](/library/jhb_dt)[[7]](/library/PhbWVt)




* Abnormal conduction of a <u>myocardial</u> impulse due to, e.g., a <u>bundle branch block</u>, conduction delay, or (according to some definitions) an <u>accessory pathway</u>

* Results in a <u>wide QRS complex</u>, as the <u>depolarization</u> of the ventricle happens more slowly (from <u>myocyte</u> to <u>myocyte</u>) rather than through rapidly conducting <u>Purkinje fibers</u>

* SVT with aberrant conduction can have a very similar appearance to <u>ventricular tachycardia</u> (see “Differentiating between VT and SVT” in “<u>Management of tachycardia</u>”).





#### Preexcitation




* Ventricular preexcitation: the premature activation of the ventricles by an <u>accessory pathway</u>

* Accessory pathway: an abnormal electrical connection outside of the <u>AV node</u> that allows for the propagation of impulses between the <u>myocardium</u> of the <u>atrium</u> and the ventricle; usually congenital, e.g., the <u>bundle of Kent</u> (see “<u>Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome</u>”), but also rarely acquired [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* Preexcitation syndrome: the combination of <u>ventricular preexcitation</u> and associated <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> (e.g., <u>AVRT</u>, <u>atrial flutter</u>, <u>atrial fibrillation</u>, <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u>); <u>WPW syndrome</u> is the most common example

* Preexcitation pattern: the typical <u>ECG</u> appearance of <u>ventricular preexcitation</u> due to abnormal conduction and <u>depolarization</u> of the ventricles

---

## Clinical features

* <u>Palpitations</u>

* Fatigue

* <u>Chest pain</u> or discomfort

* <u>Dyspnea</u>

* <u>Dizziness</u> or <u>presyncope</u>

* <u>Syncope</u> (uncommon; occurs more frequently in older adults)

* <u>Diaphoresis</u>

* Additional features seen more commonly in <u>AVNRT</u> [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[11]](/library/t2bXjG)

* Feeling of neck pounding/shirt flapping (thought to be due to <u>cannon A waves</u>)

* <u>Urinary urgency</u> and <u>polyuria</u>

* Symptom onset and resolution are typically abrupt, in contrast to <u>sinus tachycardia</u> (in which onset and resolution are more gradual).

* <u>Sudden cardiac death</u> (rare)  [[12]](/library/p11L3f0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Signs of unstable tachycardia</u> due to SVT include acute <u>pulmonary edema</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, severe <u>chest pain</u>, and <u>altered mental status</u>.

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Confirm the rhythm with a 12-lead <u>ECG</u> in all patients with new or recurrent SVT.

* Investigate the underlying cause using <u>TTE</u> and <u>laboratory studies</u> in patients with new or evolving diagnoses.

* Consider <u>ambulatory ECG</u> for with an uncertain diagnosis of <u>paroxysmal SVT</u>.

* Consider <u>EP study</u> for uncertain diagnoses that may also require <u>catheter ablation</u>.

* Consider <u>cardiac stress testing</u> for patients with <u>ASCVD risk factors</u>, suspected <u>WPW</u>, or provoked arrythmias.





> [!WARNING]
> Once the diagnosis is confirmed by <u>ECG</u>, do not delay <u>acute management of SVT</u> for additional investigations.




### Initial diagnostics [[11]](/library/t2bXjG)




* <u>ECG</u>: A 12-lead <u>ECG</u> should be performed in every patient with suspected SVT. 

* Typical features during an episode include:

* Regular rhythm; may be irregular in <u>MAT</u> or <u>atrial fibrillation</u>

* Rate > 100/minute (typically exceeds > 150/minute) [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* <u>Narrow QRS complex</u> (< 120 ms); a wide complex may be seen with <u>aberrant conduction</u>

* If findings are inconclusive, consider recording the <u>heart</u>'s electrical activity for 24–48 hours (e.g., <u>Holter monitor</u>, <u>event recorder</u>)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: to identify underlying conditions

* <u>CBC</u>: can show <u>signs of anemia</u> or infection

* <u>TSH</u>: to assess for <u>hyperthyroidism</u> and <u>hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities (e.g., <u>potassium disorders</u>, <u>calcium imbalances</u>, <u>hypomagnesemia</u>) can cause <u>arrhythmias</u>.

* <u>TTE</u> [[13]](/library/KQbUCt)

* Initial imaging modality of choice

* Potential findings include:

* Underlying structural or <u>ischemic heart disease</u>

* <u>Heart failure</u> in prolonged <u>tachycardia</u>

* Atrial <u>thrombus</u> (rare)





### Additional diagnostics [[11]](/library/t2bXjG)




Consider the following tests depending on patient <u>risk factors</u>.




* Prolonged <u>electrocardiography</u> [[14]](/library/_Nb5d8)

* Indications: patients with infrequent symptoms

* Options

* 24-hour <u>ambulatory ECG</u>: if symptoms are frequent and likely to be captured in a 24-hour period

* <u>Event recorder</u>: if patients have infrequent and mild symptoms

* <u>Implantable loop recorder</u>: for patients with infrequent and severe symptoms that impede their ability to activate the recorder

* Data is downloaded from the device, allowing for an analysis of rhythm and an evaluation of whether symptoms correlate with <u>arrhythmias</u>.

* <u>EP study</u>: with or without <u>catheter ablation</u> (<u>Gold standard</u> for diagnosing SVT; can be used for treatment)

* Indications include: uncertain diagnosis, planned <u>ablation</u>, risk <u>stratification</u>

* Disadvantages: invasive procedure, involves radiation

* Exercise tolerance testing: indicated in preexcitation (e.g., <u>risk stratification in WPW syndrome</u>) and suspected <u>catecholamine</u>-dependent <u>arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Cardiac stress testing</u>: indicated in patients with <u>ASCVD risk factors</u>

---

## Differential diagnoses

Although differentiating between types of SVT can be challenging and may require <u>EP studies</u> to confirm the diagnosis, some <u>ECG</u> features may help to differentiate diagnoses.




* <u>Sinus tachycardia</u>: most common differential; often secondary to physiologic <u>stress</u>  [[15]](/library/35YSPp)

* Other <u>narrow complex tachycardias</u> (<u>NCTs</u>): See also “<u>Differential diagnosis of SVT</u>.”

* Other <u>wide complex tachycardias</u> (<u>WCTs</u>): See also “<u>SVT with aberrancy vs. Vtach</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with SVT symptoms are frequently misdiagnosed with <u>anxiety</u> or <u>panic disorders</u>. Rule out <u>paroxysmal tachycardia</u> before making a psychiatric diagnosis to avoid <u>anchoring bias</u>.




![Tachycardia differentials](media/ot3278dk55q6ryh4vqa47yp2.jpg)

Tachycardia differentials




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

### Acute management of SVT [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[8]](/library/-UbDfG)




The underlying type of SVT is often unclear at presentation. A definitive diagnosis is not required to begin acute <u>management of tachycardia</u> following <u>ACLS</u> algorithms.




* Initiate <u>continuous cardiac monitoring</u> and <u>ECG</u> recording for all patients.

* Keep a <u>defibrillator</u> at the bedside in case rhythm and/or <u>hemodynamics</u> change (e.g., new <u>Vfib</u>).





#### Pulseless patients




* Start <u>CPR</u>.

* <u>Defibrillate</u> any <u>WCT</u> (i.e., possible <u>Vtach</u>); otherwise, treat as <u>PEA</u>.





#### Patients with <u>unstable tachycardia with pulse</u>




* Perform <u>synchronized electrical cardioversion</u> for most SVTs.

* <u>Cardioversion</u> will likely be ineffective for <u>multifocal AT</u> and <u>junctional tachycardia</u>.





#### Stable patients




Empiric management depends on QRS width and rhythm.




* SVT of unclear origin: See “<u>Management of undifferentiated SVT</u>.”

* Regular <u>NCT</u> (e.g., <u>AVNRT</u>, <u>orthodromic AVRT</u>, <u>focal AT</u>)

* Typically includes <u>vagal maneuvers</u> and <u>adenosine</u>

* See “<u>Management of stable regular NCT</u>.”

* Irregular <u>NCT</u> (e.g., <u>multifocal AT</u>, <u>Afib</u>)

* Can include <u>rate control</u>, <u>rhythm control</u>, or management of the underlying cause.

* See “<u>Management of stable irregular NCT</u>.”

* <u>WCT</u> (e.g., <u>SVT with aberrancy</u>, <u>antidromic AVRT</u>, <u>Afib with WPW</u>)

* Usually treated with <u>cardioversion</u>

* <u>AV nodal blockers</u> are best avoided.

* See “<u>Management of stable WCT</u>”.





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid using <u>AV nodal blockers</u> to treat <u>wide complex tachycardias</u>, as they may precipitate <u>Vfib</u>. [[16]](/library/Ui1bIg0)[[17]](/library/3DYSVr)




### Vagal maneuvers




* Definition: a set of actions performed to decrease the <u>heart rate</u> through physical stimulation of the <u>vagus nerve</u>

* Physiology: slows the conduction through the <u>AV node</u> (negative homotopy) and may terminate the <u>arrhythmia</u>

* Clinical application

* An important first step in acute management of most SVTs

* Avoid in <u>ventricular preexcitation</u> (due to an <u>accessory pathway</u>) with any of the following underlying <u>tachyarrhythmias</u>: <u>atrial flutter</u>, <u>atrial fibrillation</u>, <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u>, and <u>MAT</u>.





#### Valsalva maneuver




* Definition: forceful exhalation against a closed <u>airway</u>

* Technique: four phases

* Phase 1 (start strain) and phase 2 (continued strain): ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return/ventricular <u>preload</u> → ↓ <u>cardiac output</u>

* Phase 3 (release of strain) & phase 4 (recovery phase): ↓ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ <u>afterload</u> → ↑ <u>stroke volume</u> → ↑ <u>cardiac output</u>

* Applications

* Treatment of supraventricular <u>tachycardia</u> (e.g., <u>AVNRT</u>)

* Evaluate conditions of the <u>heart</u>

* Augments <u>heart sounds</u> on <u>physical exam</u> (e.g., earlier click in <u>mitral valve prolapse</u> and louder <u>murmur</u> in <u>hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy</u>)

* Decreases <u>heart sounds</u> intensity (most valve stenosis or <u>regurgitation</u> <u>murmurs</u>)

* Test for <u>hernia</u> or <u>varicocele</u> (increased intraabdominal pressure → bulging)

* Diagnosis of urinary <u>stress incontinence</u> (urine leakage during the maneuver)

* Measure to normalize middle-<u>ear</u> pressure (e.g., in diving)

* Contraindications: include recent <u>myocardial infarction</u>, <u>aortic stenosis</u>, and <u>glaucoma</u>. [[18]](/library/NDY-er)





##### Modified Valsalva maneuver [[18]](/library/NDY-er)




* Patient sits in a semirecumbent position

* Blows into a 10 mL syringe for 15 seconds (moving the plunger up achieves a strain of ∼ 40 mm Hg) [[19]](/library/K5bUO8)

* Afterwards the patient is laid <u>supine</u> and the legs are passively elevated to 45° for 15 seconds.

* Return to the semirecumbent position for 45 seconds before reassessing rhythm





#### Carotid sinus massage [[20]](/library/u5bpN8)




* Listen first to ensure there are no <u>carotid bruits</u> (if present, select another <u>vagal maneuver</u>).  [[21]](/library/E5b8N8)

* Apply steady pressure at the level of the carotid bifurcation on one side for 10–15 seconds.

* If there is no response, the process can be repeated using the <u>contralateral</u> <u>carotid sinus</u>.

* <u>Carotid sinus massage</u> stimulates the <u>baroreceptors</u> → stimulates <u>CN IX</u> (specifically the branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve to the carotid sinus) → nerve impulse transmission to the medulla (<u>nucleus tractus solitarius</u>) → efferent signals from the medulla to the <u>myocardium</u> via the <u>vagus nerve</u> (<u>parasympathetic</u> supply) → ↓ <u>AVN</u> conduction, ↓ <u>heart</u> rate, ↓ contractility, and <u>vasodilation</u> (↓ blood pressure; may cause <u>presyncope</u> or <u>syncope</u>) → termination of <u>arrhythmia</u>





#### Diving reflex




* Traditionally involves immersing the head in cold water, which is uncomfortable for most patients

* Can be limited to applying a bag of ice water to the face (particularly the forehead and nasal area) for ∼ 10 seconds  [[22]](/library/GKaB3l)





> [!WARNING]
> Do not simultaneously apply bilateral carotid <u>artery</u> pressure because this can impede <u>cerebral blood flow</u>.




### Pharmacotherapy




* See “<u>Management of undifferentiated SVT</u>” for a general algorithm.

* Definitive pharmacotherapy depends on the underlying rhythm.

* See “<u>Treatment of AVNRT</u>.”

* See “<u>Treatment of AVRT</u>.”

* See “<u>Treatment of WPW</u>.”

* See “<u>Treatment of focal AT</u>.”

* See “<u>Treatment of MAT</u>.”

* See “<u>Management of Afib with RVR</u>.”

* See “<u>Treatment of junctional tachycardia</u>.”





### Catheter ablation




* Description

* Radiofrequency or cryothermal energy is applied via a cardiac catheter to eliminate aberrant pathways or impulses from arrhythmogenic foci.

* Usually performed in conjunction with an <u>EP study</u>

* Indications [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* Curative therapy in <u>AVNRT</u>, <u>AVRT</u> with concealed pathway, or drug-refractory AT

* Symptomatic patients who want to avoid long-term drug therapy (especially younger patients)

* Asymptomatic patients with special lifestyle considerations (e.g., pilots)





### Further management and disposition [[23]](/library/KnbU88)




* Successful <u>cardioversion</u>: Consider discharge after a period of monitoring if clinically stable and no other acute medical issues.

* Unsuccessful <u>cardioversion</u>

* Urgent cardiology consult for specialist treatment, e.g., a second dose of <u>cardioversion</u>, antiarrhythmic infusion

* Admit to critical care unit for further management.

* Other indications for hospital admission

* Possible <u>ischemic</u> event

* Any VT or unstable rhythm (even if terminated)

* Any <u>LOC</u>

* Possible <u>preexcitation syndrome</u>

## Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia

### Definition



* A <u>tachyarrhythmia</u> caused by a dysfunctional <u>AV node</u> that contains two electrical pathways, which form a reentry circuit




### Pathophysiology




* The <u>AV node</u> contains two electrical pathways, one fast and one slow → the electrical impulse circles around the <u>AV node</u> within both pathways → a continuous circuit conducts impulses to the ventricles → <u>tachycardia</u>

* Approx. 90% of cases are due to anterograde conduction across the slow-conducting pathway and retrograde conduction in the fast pathway (although the reverse is possible).





![Pathophysiology of typical atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)](media/ryso4djvece1mlsv7pqa39nh.jpg)

Pathophysiology of typical atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)




#### ECG findings in AVNRT [[24]](/library/uTbpsG)[[25]](/library/vTbAsG)




<u>ECG</u> may be normal between episodes of <u>tachycardia</u>. Findings may be indistinguishable from those of <u>orthodromic AVRT</u> and include:




* <u>Heart rate</u> typically 150–220/minute

* Typically <u>narrow QRS complexes</u> (a <u>wide QRS complex</u> may be seen if there is <u>aberrant conduction</u>)

* Regular rhythm

* <u>P wave</u> is typically not visible (it falls in or is "buried" in the <u>QRS complex</u>)





![Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)](media/r6gt6qmcucopkgn2cykg7hsd.jpg)

Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)

![Atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT)](media/ky5jv8vimq0drzsal80dyl2f.jpg)

Atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT)

![Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)](media/hnuy4xbud9i11lzm8cgzc4uh.jpg)

Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)

![Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)](media/sma8s009cv9686hjd8btf4ji.jpg)

Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT)




### Treatment of AVNRT




#### Acute management




* <u>Unstable tachycardia with a pulse</u>: <u>electrical cardioversion</u>

* Stable with <u>narrow QRS complex</u>: See “<u>Management of stable regular NCT</u>.”

* First step: <u>vagal maneuvers</u>

* If SVT persists: intravenous medical therapy

* First-line: <u>adenosine</u> (if no <u>contraindications to adenosine</u> present)

* Other options: <u>calcium channel blockers</u> (e.g., <u>verapamil</u>, <u>diltiazem</u>) or <u>beta blockers</u> (e.g., <u>metoprolol</u>)

* Stable with <u>wide QRS complex</u> (suspected <u>aberrant conduction</u>): See “<u>Management of stable WCT</u>.”

* Established diagnosis of <u>AVNRT</u>: <u>AV nodal blocking agents</u> are generally safe.  [[26]](/library/HNbKc8)

* Uncertain diagnosis of <u>AVNRT</u>: Avoid <u>AV nodal blocking agents</u>.





#### Long-term management




* Infrequent and mild episodes: may be managed with self-guided <u>vagal maneuvers</u>.

* First line: percutaneous <u>catheter ablation</u> of the slow pathway  [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[27]](/library/pgbLwG)

* Second line: pharmacological therapy  [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* Daily medication options

* <u>Beta blockers</u>, e.g., <u>propranolol</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* <u>Verapamil</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* <u>Diltiazem</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* <u>Pill-in-the-pocket</u> regimens (<u>off-label</u>) [[28]](/library/KgbUwG)

* <u>Propranolol</u> DOSAGE PLUS <u>diltiazem</u> DOSAGE [[28]](/library/KgbUwG)

* OR <u>flecainide</u> DOSAGE  [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[28]](/library/KgbUwG)

---

## Atrioventricular reciprocating tachycardia

### Definition




* A <u>tachyarrhythmia</u> caused by an <u>accessory pathway</u> that creates a reentrant circuit with the <u>AV node</u>

* <u>Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome</u> is a common cause of <u>AVRT</u> but they are not synonymous.  [[11]](/library/t2bXjG)





### Pathophysiology  [[11]](/library/t2bXjG)[[29]](/library/JgbswG)




* Orthodromic AVRT (most common; 90–95%) [[30]](/library/BDYzgr)

* Antegrade conduction (<u>atrium</u> → ventricle) through <u>AV node</u> (<u>narrow QRS complex</u>); retrograde conduction (ventricle → <u>atrium</u>) through <u>accessory pathway</u>

* Can occur with a concealed or manifest pathway

* On rare occasions, occurs almost incessantly as a result of a concealed, posteroseptal pathway (permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia; <u>PJRT</u>)  [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[31]](/library/embxe8)

* Antidromic AVRT (rare; 5–10%) [[32]](/library/K2bUiG)

* Antegrade conduction (<u>atrium</u> → ventricle) through <u>accessory pathway</u>; retrograde conduction (ventricle → <u>atrium</u>) through <u>AV node</u>

* <u>Wide QRS complex</u>, as ventricular <u>depolarization</u> happens slowly from <u>myocyte</u> to <u>myocyte</u> rather than through the rapid <u>His-Purkinje system</u>

* Only occurs with a manifest pathway





> [!NOTE]
> <u>AVRT</u> is caused by an <u>accessory pathway</u>, whereas in AVNRT there are two functional pathways within the AV node.




![Orthodromic and antidromic AVRT](media/m1xf85bcfniwtjdpapqjr5fe.jpg)

Orthodromic and antidromic AVRT




### <u>ECG</u> findings




| <br>ECG findings in AVRT [[11]](/library/t2bXjG)[[33]](/library/XUb9bG)[[34]](/library/qgbCwG)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Orthodromic AVRT</u> | <br><br>* <u>Heart rate</u> 150–250/minute<br><br>* Regular rhythm<br><br>* <u>Narrow QRS complex</u><br><br>* <u>P wave</u> typically follows <u>QRS complex</u>.<br><br>* Because the AP is conducting in a retrograde direction, there is no visible delta wave during the <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>.<br><br>* Can be indistinguishable from <u>AVNRT</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Antidromic AVRT</u> | <br><br>* <u>Heart rate</u> 150–250/minute<br><br>* Regular rhythm<br><br>* <u>Wide QRS complex</u> (similar in appearance to <u>ventricular tachycardia</u>, preexcited <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u>, and preexcited <u>atrial flutter</u>)<br><br>* Shortened <u>PR interval</u><br><br>* The morphology of the <u>QRS complex</u> means that the delta wave is frequently not visible during the <u>tachyarrhythmia</u>.<br><br><br> |





### Treatment of AVRT




#### Acute episodes




* <u>Unstable tachycardia with a pulse</u>: <u>electrical cardioversion</u>

* Stable <u>orthodromic AVRT</u>: See “<u>Management of stable regular NCT</u>.”

* First step: <u>vagal maneuvers</u>

* If SVT persists: intravenous medical therapy

* First-line: <u>adenosine</u> (if there are no <u>contraindications to adenosine</u>)

* Other options: <u>calcium channel blockers</u> (e.g., <u>verapamil</u>, <u>diltiazem</u>) or <u>beta blockers</u> (e.g., <u>metoprolol</u>)

* Stable <u>antidromic AVRT</u> (<u>wide QRS complex</u>): See “<u>Management of stable WCT</u>.”

* Established diagnosis of <u>AVRT</u>: <u>AV nodal blocking agents</u> are safe.

* Uncertain diagnosis of <u>AVRT</u>: Avoid <u>AV nodal blocking agents</u>.





#### Long-term management [[2]](/library/2FYThI)




* First-line: <u>catheter ablation</u>

* Pharmacotherapy for AVRT: for patients who are not candidates for <u>ablation</u> or who prefer medication

* Treatment depends on whether a <u>preexcitation pattern</u> is seen on <u>ECG</u> (options include <u>sotalol</u>, <u>flecainide</u>; , and <u>propafenone</u>). [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* <u>Preexcitation pattern</u> is visible. 

* Known <u>heart</u> disease: <u>sotalol</u> DOSAGE  OR <u>dofetilide</u> DOSAGE

* No known <u>heart</u> disease: <u>flecainide</u> DOSAGE OR <u>propafenone</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Preexcitation pattern</u> is not visible. 

* <u>CCBs</u>: <u>verapamil</u> DOSAGE OR <u>diltiazem</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Beta blockers</u>: <u>propranolol</u> DOSAGE OR <u>metoprolol</u> DOSAGE

* Alternative: : Consider <u>amiodarone</u> if no other treatments are effective or if all are contraindicated.

---

## Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome

### Definitions




* <u>Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome</u>:  (<u>WPW</u>): a congenital condition characterized by intermittent tachycardias and signs of <u>ventricular preexcitation</u> on <u>ECG</u>, both of which arise from an <u>accessory pathway</u> known as the bundle of Kent

* Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern: characteristic signs of <u>ventricular preexcitation</u> on <u>ECG</u> with no evidence of <u>arrhythmia</u> and no reported symptoms [[35]](/library/plXLBy)





### Pathophysiology




* A congenital <u>accessory pathway</u>, the <u>bundle of Kent</u>, connects the <u>atria</u> and ventricles, bypassing the AV node and leading to <u>ventricular preexcitation</u>.

* May be associated with structural abnormalities of the <u>heart</u>, in particular <u>Ebstein anomaly</u> [[36]](/library/J2bsiG)

* ∼ 10% of patients have multiple accessory pathways (more common with coexisting <u>structural heart disease</u>).  [[35]](/library/plXLBy)[[37]](/library/H2bKQG)

* May be asymptomatic (<u>WPW pattern</u>) or associated with <u>arrhythmias</u> (<u>WPW syndrome</u>), including: [[36]](/library/J2bsiG)

* <u>AVRT</u> (most common; 80%)

* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u> (15–35%; <u>incidence</u> increases with age)

* <u>Atrial flutter</u> (5%)

* Others (rare): <u>MAT</u>, <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u>, <u>ventricular fibrillation</u>





![Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome and pattern](media/j741dvmk3hl0rfrtwmzwqq8j.jpg)

Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome and pattern




### <u>Epidemiology</u>




* The <u>prevalence</u> of <u>WPW pattern</u> is 0.1–0.2% in the general population and 0.55% in first-degree relatives. [[38]](/library/6lXjBy)

* A <u>proportion</u> of these cases is due to familial <u>WPW syndrome</u>, a rare <u>autosomal-dominant</u> genetic disorder that causes conduction abnormalities and <u>hypertrophic cardiomyopathy</u>. [[39]](/library/G2bBQG)

* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> [[40]](/library/nyb7fw)

* Symptoms typically develop at 20–40 years of age. [[36]](/library/J2bsiG)





### ECG findings in WPW




* While in <u>sinus rhythm</u>, a <u>preexcitation pattern</u> may be present.  [[9]](/library/p2bLiG)

* Short <u>PR interval</u>

* ECG delta wave: a slurred upstroke at the start of the <u>QRS complex</u>, secondary to preexcitation

* Widened QRS

* Can show any of the <u>arrhythmias</u> associated with <u>WPW</u> [[36]](/library/J2bsiG)

* See “<u>ECG findings in AVRT</u>.”

* See “<u>WPW with atrial fibrillation</u>.”





![Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome](media/vaxzoedvv3poprch1esjdtzs.jpg)

Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome

![Delta wave](media/wt79rlhpum8r1uqvu1ihljkc.jpg)

Delta wave

![Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome with atrial fibrillation (1/2)](media/n6nhdrgja161ywsak6kbsq5g.jpg)

Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome with atrial fibrillation (1/2)

![Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome after conversion from atrial fibrillation (2/2)](media/ec6r729fxkn078f0569elfc9.jpg)

Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome after conversion from atrial fibrillation (2/2)




### Treatment of WPW [[8]](/library/-UbDfG)




#### Acute episodes




* <u>Unstable tachycardia with a pulse</u>: <u>electrical cardioversion</u>

* Stable: Assess underlying rhythm.

* Regular <u>NCT</u> (i.e., <u>orthodromic AVRT</u>): <u>vagal maneuvers</u>, <u>adenosine</u>; see “<u>Management of stable regular NCT</u>”

* <u>WCT</u>: irregular (e.g., underlying <u>Afib</u> or <u>multifocal AT</u>) OR regular (underlying <u>Aflut</u> or <u>focal AT</u>)  [[8]](/library/-UbDfG)

* Avoid <u>AV nodal blocking agents</u> and <u>vagal maneuvers</u> (may precipitate <u>Vtach</u> or <u>Vfib</u>)

* <u>Rhythm control</u> measures (i.e., <u>cardioversion</u> or IV <u>procainamide</u>) are the safest treatment option.

* See “<u>Management of stable WCT</u>” and ”<u>Management of preexcited Afib</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>AV nodal blocking agents</u> and <u>vagal maneuvers</u> for the following <u>preexcited tachycardias</u>: <u>Afib</u>, <u>Aflut</u>, <u>focal AT</u>, and <u>MAT</u>.




#### Long-term management of WPW [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[40]](/library/nyb7fw)




Management of <u>WPW pattern</u> and <u>WPW syndrome</u> depends on underlying <u>risk factors</u> and patient preference.




##### Risk stratification in WPW syndrome [[41]](/library/Rhbldt)




Risk <u>stratification</u> is determined by a cardiologist based on clinical, <u>ECG</u>, and electrophysiological parameters.




* Concerning clinical features

* <u>Syncope</u>

* Associated <u>atrial fibrillation</u>, <u>atrial flutter</u>, or <u>atrial tachycardia</u>

* Aborted <u>sudden cardiac death</u>

* Dynamic <u>ECG</u> testing: e.g., ambulatory <u>Holter monitoring</u> or <u>exercise stress testing</u> to assess for evidence of intermittency or loss of preexcitation  [[42]](/library/wfbhoG)

* <u>EP studies</u> 

* Indicated in patients with:

* Concerning clinical features

* No evidence of intermittency or loss of preexcitation signs

* High-risk occupations (e.g., pilots, athletes)

* Allows the length of the <u>refractory period</u> to be determined  [[41]](/library/Rhbldt)





##### High-risk patients




<u>Catheter ablation</u> of the <u>accessory pathway</u> should be offered to all patients. [[2]](/library/2FYThI)




##### Low-risk patients [[2]](/library/2FYThI)




* Asymptomatic: usually no treatment required

* Symptomatic

* First-line: <u>catheter ablation</u>

* Second-line (e.g., <u>ablation</u> contraindicated or declined): long-term <u>antiarrhythmics</u> in consultation with a cardiologist

* No <u>structural heart disease</u>: Consider <u>flecainide</u> OR <u>propafenone</u>. [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* <u>Structural heart disease</u>

* Consider <u>dofetilide</u> OR <u>sotalol</u>

* Use <u>AV nodal blockers</u> with caution.

## Focal atrial tachycardia

### Definition




* <u>Focal atrial tachycardia</u> (FAT; <u>focal AT</u>): a supraventricular <u>tachycardia</u> that arises from a localized atrial focus outside of the <u>SA node</u> [[2]](/library/2FYThI)

* Atrial tachycardia (AT): an umbrella term for <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u> and <u>multifocal atrial tachycardia</u> (<u>MAT</u>) that is often used synonymously with <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u>





### Etiology [[15]](/library/35YSPp)




* <u>Idiopathic</u>: most common

* Chronic conditions: <u>hypertension</u>, <u>heart</u> disease, <u>cardiomyopathy</u>

* Acute conditions: <u>myocardial infarction</u>, infection, <u>alcohol poisoning</u>

* Drug toxicity

* <u>Digoxin</u> (most common)

* <u>Theophylline</u>

* <u>Cocaine</u>





### Pathophysiology [[43]](/library/tUbXUG)[[44]](/library/zUbrfG)




* Possible mechanisms [[45]](/library/4fb3mG)

* <u>Triggered activity</u>: a result of <u>early afterdepolarizations</u> (EAD) or <u>delayed afterdepolarization</u> (DAD)

* Microreentry: slow conduction at discrete regions of <u>fibrotic</u> cardiac tissue

* Enhanced <u>automaticity</u>: <u>acceleration</u> of a normal automatic pacemaker  [[46]](/library/1fb2OG)

* Key features

* Originates outside of the <u>SA node</u>

* Abrupt onset

* Can be sustained or nonsustained

* Worsened by adrenergic activity





### ECG findings in focal AT [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[46]](/library/1fb2OG)




* <u>Heart rate</u> 100–250/minute  [[46]](/library/1fb2OG)

* Regular rhythm

* Can have 1:1 or 2:1 AV conduction

* <u>P wave</u>

* Typically visible in 2:1 AT

* May be hidden by the <u>QRS complex</u> or <u>T wave</u> in 1:1 AT

* The morphology depends on the site of origin but remains constant.

* An isoelectric baseline is present between <u>P waves</u>.

* <u>QRS complex</u>: morphology does not vary

* Narrow complex: most common

* <u>Wide QRS complex</u> may be present in <u>SVT with aberrant conduction</u>.





> [!TIP]
> An isoelectric baseline between <u>P waves</u> can help distinguish <u>focal AT</u> from <u>atrial flutter</u>. [[8]](/library/-UbDfG)




![Nonsustained focal atrial tachycardia](media/j4xhfrimexeg8ntdxnzxfxol.jpg)

Nonsustained focal atrial tachycardia




### Treatment of focal AT [[2]](/library/2FYThI)




#### Acute episodes




Episodes of <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u> are most commonly <u>self-limiting</u> and asymptomatic, in which case they do not require treatment.




* <u>Unstable tachycardia with a pulse</u>: <u>electrical cardioversion</u>

* Stable

* <u>Narrow QRS complex</u>

* First step: <u>vagal maneuvers</u>

* If SVT persists: intravenous medical therapy

* First-line if there are no <u>contraindications to adenosine</u> and diagnosis of <u>focal AT</u> is not established: <u>adenosine</u>

* First-line if diagnosis of <u>focal AT</u> is established: <u>calcium channel blockers</u> (e.g., <u>verapamil</u>, <u>diltiazem</u>) or <u>beta blockers</u> (e.g., <u>metoprolol</u>)

* See “<u>Management of undifferentiated SVT</u>” for details.

* <u>Wide QRS complex</u> (suspected <u>aberrant conduction</u>)

* Preexcited <u>focal AT</u> ruled out: <u>AV nodal blocking agents</u> are generally safe.

* Preexcited <u>focal AT</u> possible: Avoid <u>AV nodal blocking agents</u>.

* See “<u>Stable, wide-complex tachycardia</u>” for details.

* All patients: Identify and treat acute reversible underlying conditions (see “Etiology”).





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>AV nodal blockers</u> in patients with preexcited <u>focal atrial tachycardia</u> (e.g., due to <u>WPW</u>) because they can trigger <u>ventricular arrhythmias</u>.




#### Long-term management




* <u>Catheter ablation</u>: for symptomatic patients who are candidates (e.g., refractory AT, younger age, focal atrial <u>tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy</u>) or those who prefer it as an alternative to pharmacotherapy  [[47]](/library/dfboOG)[[48]](/library/kfbmmG)

* Pharmacotherapy

* <u>Beta blockers</u>: e.g., <u>metoprolol</u> DOSAGE

* <u>CCBs</u>: <u>verapamil</u> DOSAGE OR <u>diltiazem</u> DOSAGE

* A cardiology consultation is required if the following medications are being considered:

* <u>Class Ic antiarrhythmic</u> drugs : <u>flecainide</u> DOSAGE OR <u>propafenone</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Class III antiarrhythmic drugs</u> : <u>amiodarone</u> DOSAGE  OR <u>sotalol</u> DOSAGE

* Pacemaker implantation: Consider for patients with refractory symptoms after unsuccessful invasive and medical therapy.

* <u>Surgery</u> (e.g., left atrial isolation): less common since the advancement of <u>catheter ablation</u> [[49]](/library/_Ub5fG)

* Other

* Management of underlying conditions (see “Etiology”)

* Anticoagulation: not indicated in the absence of coexisting <u>arrhythmia</u>.

---

## Multifocal atrial tachycardia

### Definition



* An irregular SVT featuring ≥ 3 morphologies of <u>P waves</u> [[2]](/library/2FYThI)




### Etiology [[50]](/library/lUbvWG)[[51]](/library/lfbvmG)




* Severe underlying conditions (e.g., <u>heart failure</u> and pulmonary diseases, such as <u>COPD</u> or <u>pneumonia</u>)

* Drugs (e.g., <u>theophylline</u>, <u>isoproterenol</u>) [[52]](/library/Nfb-mG)

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities (e.g., <u>hypokalemia</u>, <u>hypomagnesemia</u>)

* Other: <u>hypoxia</u>, <u>hypercapnia</u>, <u>acidosis</u>, <u>dysautonomia</u>





### Pathophysiology [[53]](/library/4Ub3WG)




* Multifocal origin of pacemaker activity

* Mechanism remains unclear  [[50]](/library/lUbvWG)

* Often associated with <u>right atrial enlargement</u>





### ECG findings in MAT [[50]](/library/lUbvWG)




* <u>Heart rate</u> 100–200/minute

* Irregularly irregular rhythm

* <u>P waves</u>

* Three or more varying morphologies

* Separated by an isoelectric baseline

* Variable <u>PR interval</u>

* <u>QRS complex</u>: morphology does not vary

* <u>Narrow QRS complex</u>: most common

* <u>Wide QRS complex</u> may be present in <u>aberrant conduction</u>

* May progress to <u>atrial fibrillation</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Do not confuse <u>MAT</u> with <u>atrial fibrillation</u>. In <u>Afib</u>, there are no distinct or organized <u>P waves</u>, whereas in <u>MAT</u> there are distinct <u>P waves</u> with varying morphologies.




> [!TIP]
> Unlike in <u>atrial flutter</u>, in <u>MAT</u> there are distinct isoelectric intervals between <u>P waves</u>.




![Multifocal atrial tachycardia](media/vi6cajsyhz8xntaqr2wgeqw8.jpg)

Multifocal atrial tachycardia




### Treatment of multifocal atrial tachycardia [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[11]](/library/t2bXjG)[[54]](/library/NUb-WG)




<u>Treatment of MAT</u> is challenging and specialists should be involved early. Patients often have severe underlying conditions and <u>rhythm control</u> and <u>electrical cardioversion</u> are not effective. For clinically-oriented management algorithms for patients with <u>tachycardia</u>, see “<u>Management of tachycardia</u>”.




* First-line treatment: management of underlying causes [[55]](/library/mfbV5G)

* Manage exacerbations of chronic diseases (see “Etiology” above).

* Correct reversible conditions, e.g., <u>hypoxemia</u>, <u>acidosis</u>, <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities.

* See “<u>Potassium replacement</u>” and “<u>Magnesium replacement</u>.”

* Discontinue potential offending medications.

* IV <u>magnesium</u> DOSAGE may be helpful even in patients with normal <u>magnesium</u> levels. [[17]](/library/3DYSVr)

* <u>Rate control</u> 

* <u>Beta blockers</u>: e.g., <u>metoprolol</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Calcium channel blockers</u> : <u>verapamil</u> DOSAGE

* <u>AV node radiofrequency ablation</u>: Consider in refractory <u>MAT</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>AV nodal blockers</u> in patients with preexcited <u>MAT</u> (e.g., due to <u>WPW</u>) because of the risk of <u>ventricular arrhythmias</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>electrical cardioversion</u> and <u>antiarrhythmic drugs</u> (e.g., <u>procainamide</u>, <u>lidocaine</u>, <u>phenytoin</u>), as they are not effective in treating <u>MAT</u>. [[2]](/library/2FYThI)[[54]](/library/NUb-WG)
